                                 COMMENTS OF
            THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF MISSOURI

           Pursuant to Rule 2061 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (Commission or FERC), the Public Service Commission of the State of

Missouri (Missouri PSC) submits the following comments in response to a complaint filed by

Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (NIPSCO) filed against the Midcontinent

Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) in this docket.



                                   I. Service and Communication

                                               II. Background

        The Public Service Commission of the State of Missouri (Missouri PSC) is a “state

commission” as defined in Section 1.101(k) of the Commission’s Rules of General

Applicability.2 Missouri law authorizes the Missouri PSC to regulate rates, charges and terms of

service for the sale and distribution of electricity by public utilities to consumers in the state.3

Missouri has retained a vertically integrated regulatory structure. Public utilities under the

jurisdiction of the Missouri PSC are required to provide service to their customers that is “safe

and adequate and in all respects just and reasonable.”4

        The Missouri PSC has approved electrical corporations under its jurisdiction to be

members of two Regional Transmission Organizations (RTOs): the Midcontinent Independent

System Operator, Inc. (MISO) and the Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP). Ameren Missouri, a

MISO member, serves St. Louis and portions of eastern, central, and northwestern Missouri.

Evergy Missouri Metro and Evergy Missouri West, serving Kansas City and western Missouri,

and The Empire District Electric Co. d/b/a Liberty, serving southwest Missouri, are members of

SPP.

        In its complaint, NIPSCO requests a Commission order directing MISO to establish a rate

schedule under its Open Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff

(Tariff) that would provide a mechanism for NIPSCO to recover all costs associated with

NIPSCO’s compliance with a recent order (DOE Order) from the U.S. Secretary of

Energy (Secretary).5 In the DOE Order, the Secretary determined that the continued operation

of NIPSCO’s R.M. Schahfer Generating Station Units 17 and 18 (Schahfer Units) beyond their

                                      III. Summary of Comments

        The Secretary’s continued use of FPA Section 202(c) to keep power plants operating past

their planned retirement date raises important questions for state commissions that traditionally

oversee plant retirements. In these comments, the Missouri PSC reiterates the need for FERC to

direct MISO to convene a stakeholder process to develop a tariff to address 202(c) orders. The

Missouri PSC also urges FERC to require NIPSCO and other owners of plants subject to 202(c)

orders to provide regular reports on the costs of compliance with such orders. The Missouri PSC

appreciates the opportunity to comment on this complaint.7



                                 IV. Comments of the Missouri PSC

A.      The continued use of Section 202(c) orders provides new justification for

stakeholder involvement in cost allocation.

        This case is similar to the complaint filed against MISO by Consumers Energy in FERC

Docket No. EL25-90. In that case, the Organization of MISO States, Inc. (OMS) and the

Missouri PSC predicted that the DOE would issue more 202(c) orders in MISO, and urged the

Commission to direct MISO to convene a stakeholder process to produce a tariff to proactively

address 202(c) orders. In that case, NIPSCO asked FERC to initiate a 206 proceeding at MISO to



6
  Id. at pg. 5.
7
  The Missouri PSC has also signed and endorses the comments of the Organization of MISO States, Inc. (OMS) in
this docket.

                                                       3
 establish a tariff for 202(c) orders, instead of leaving them to be addressed “in a piecemeal

fashion.”8

        In the Consumers Energy case, the Commission found that further process was not

necessary, because “the most reasonable reading of the DOE Order’s intended scope is that the

emergency necessitating the continued operation of the Campbell Plant is in Local Resource

Zones 1-7.”9 This reasoning no longer applies, however, as this DOE Order finds an “emergency

situation” in MISO more broadly, drawing on MISO’s revised resource adequacy construct, the

results of the voluntary OMS-MISO survey, and the need to power data centers to support a

finding of a “potential longer term resource adequacy emergency in MISO.”10 These issues

pertain to all of MISO, while this DOE Order makes only passing reference to Local Resource

Zones 1-7.

        This DOE Order thus broadens its definition of “emergency” to encompass longer-term

resource planning issues that encroach further into state resource adequacy jurisdiction. This

more expansive DOE Order justifies a more comprehensive approach at MISO. The Commission

should acknowledge the fact that the DOE’s 202(c) orders are not “one-offs,” and direct MISO to

initiate a stakeholder process and develop a tariff to meet that reality.

 B.        Stakeholders and consumers are entitled to more transparency about the ongoing

use and costs of the DOE’s 202(c) orders.

          The transparency of the costs imposed on consumers falls squarely within the issue of

cost allocation that the DOE has delegated to FERC under its 202(c) orders.11 Under the Federal

Power Act and state law, state commissions like the Missouri PSC retain authority to decide

what amount and what type of resources constitute safe and adequate service, and how much

retail customers in their jurisdictions should pay for that service.12 As the DOE expands its use of

202(c) orders and their scope to encompass more issues of state-jurisdictional resource planning,

the Commission should use its cost allocation authority to ensure that state planners and

consumers in MISO have timely information about the use and costs of plants subject to 202(c)

orders.

          Commission precedent supports heightened transparency requirements when resources

are used outside normal operations. For example, in 2006 the Commission approved

“Exceptional Dispatch” provisions to authorize the California Independent System Operator

(CAISO) to manually commit and/or dispatch resources in order to maintain reliable grid

operations under unusual and infrequent circumstances.13 The Commission ordered CAISO to

make reports every 60 days detailing the “frequency, volume, costs, causes and degree of

mitigation of exceptional dispatches.”14 The Commission found that regular reporting would

“provide the necessary transparency to enable stakeholders to remain informed about the use of

Exceptional Dispatch… .”15 The Commission further found that frequent, transparent reporting

 “should help facilitate any stakeholder processes concerning the development of additional

market mechanisms to address situations that frequently give rise to exceptional dispatches.”16

           Similarly, additional transparency about the use and costs of plants subject to 202(c)

emergency orders will help MISO stakeholders better understand how such orders mitigate

resource adequacy concerns. As the DOE Order notes, MISO and its stakeholders have

implemented new tariff provisions, like the Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS), to

address reliability needs.17 More transparency about the costs and benefits of these 202(c) orders

will help MISO and its stakeholders evaluate new approaches to reliability, and will be of

particular benefit to state commissions as they evaluate the retirement of power plants within

their jurisdictions. On this basis, FERC should direct NIPSCO and other owners of plants subject

to 202(c) orders to submit regular reports into these cost allocation dockets about the plants’

continued operations and their costs, subject to appropriate confidentiality provisions.



                                             V. Conclusion

           The Missouri PSC respectfully submits these comments.
